transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-12 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~68 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Alex (Redwood SRE); Dr. Lila Chen, Tom A., Sara O., Jamal R. (MedTech)

[00:00] Jordan Park: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. We're gonna do a deep dive on long context performance — 128k plus workloads — mostly Maya and Alex will drive the tech details. Lila, Tom, anything you wanna call out before we jump in?
[00:18] Dr. Lila Chen: no, just that our main goal is being able to ingest full patient histories and run multi-hop QA with context windows up to 128k tokens. Latency targets ideally sub-2s for short queries against a single record but we know that's tough.
[00:35] Tom Alvarez: also want to highlight network constraints in our VPC, and we have strict egress rules. So on-prem or VPC only, no public endpoints.
[00:44] Maya Singh: great, we'll cover VPC/private deployment considerations. Quick agenda: chunking/serializing, KV cache behavior, batching, quant, attention kernels, and benchmark plan.
[01:05] Alex Ramos: can I add monitoring/observability too? token-level latency breakdowns, cache hit/miss metrics, that kind of stuff.
[01:12] Jordan Park: yep add that. ok Maya, take it away.

---

[01:30] Maya Singh: cool, so starting with chunking strategies. For 128k plus contexts we generally see two dominant approaches: fixed-size chunking (sliding windows or non-overlap) and semantic chunking (sentence/section boundaries, embeddings-based cut). Fixed is simpler and cheaper but can split important spans; semantic preserves meaning but requires upfront embedding/index cost. In practice we recommend a hybrid: coarse semantic boundaries, then fixed sub-chunks for attention-friendly sizes.
[02:10] Dr. Lila Chen: when you say fixed sub-chunks, what's typical size? 4k? 8k?
[02:16] Maya Singh: in our bench we use 8k to 16k sub-chunks paired with an async reassembly step. For 128k contexts we usually create ~8-16 sub-chunks depending on tokenization density. That keeps KV cache entries manageable.
[02:34] Jamal Reed: does that reassembly add latency for QA?
[02:38] Maya Singh: it adds some overhead, yes — typically a few hundred ms to 1s depending on how many chunks you need to merge. We do progressive retrieval and respond with partials when possible to meet SLAs.

[03:05] Tom Alvarez: curious about cache size: if we keep KV cache for all 128k tokens that's huge, right? what's practical?
[03:12] Alex Ramos: yeah, fully materializing KV for 128k at once consumes memory proportional to seq_len * hidden_size. On A100/8x it's feasible but expensive. Redwood approach is sharded KV + tiered caching: hot prefixes stay in fast GPU memory, older segments spill to CPU or NVMe cache. We also support evictions based on recency or semantic importance.
[03:40] Maya Singh: to add, we support chunk-level caching — cache summaries/embeddings for blocks so you can avoid re-attending to full raw tokens for repeated queries. That's a big win for throughput on QA workloads.

[04:05] Dr. Lila Chen: how consistent is spillover? if NVMe is used, does that blow out latency for some queries?
[04:12] Alex Ramos: spike risk exists; that's why we recommend benchmarking with your access patterns. We have policies to prefetch likely-needed chunks into GPU memory based on query affinity. Peak tail latency can be controlled with pre-warming and larger hot-set configs.

[04:40] [05:00] Maya Singh: next, batching and continuous batching. For these workloads throughput matters — we recommend continuous batching with small-time windows (10-50ms) for mergeable requests. But for single-record interactive queries you must favor latency: set batch windows to near-zero and rely on cache hits to keep tokens generated from GPU. We exposed a knob for max_batch_delay and dynamic scaling for latency SLOs.
[05:30] Tom Alvarez: how do you reconcile continuous batching with per-customer isolation? we are multi-tenant within our infra.
[05:38] Maya Singh: Redwood Dedicated supports per-queue isolation and weighted scheduling. For private deployments we can allocate dedicated pools per tenant or per route. Batching respects tenant isolation, we don't mix tokens across isolation boundaries unless explicit shared pools are configured.

[06:05] [06:20] Jordan Park: can we talk quantization trade-offs — we know MedTech is sensitive about accuracy for clinical QA.
[06:28] Maya Singh: absolutely. Quantization options: Q8/Q4/Q5 variants; we also support per-layer mixed quant and GPTQ-style calibration. In our internal tests Q4_0 with per-channel scales gives ~1-3% quality delta on NLU metrics vs fp16 but 2-3x throughput. Q5_0 and some 3-bit schemes yield larger deltas; depends on eval set. For clinical workloads we often suggest running a dedicated eval suite and gating quant levels by regression thresholds.
[07:00] Dr. Lila Chen: do you provide tooling to run those regressions?
[07:04] Maya Singh: yes, Redwood Optimize includes eval harnesses and you can tie alerts to prompt sets so any regression triggers an alert and rollback. We'll share the notebook and a sample eval set.

[07:30] [07:45] Alex Ramos: on kernel-level attention optimizations: we support FlashAttention (when model weights are compatible), blocked attention, and a grouped-query optimization for retrieval-heavy patterns. For very long contexts sparse attention or locality-biased attention (ALiBi-like) can reduce compute. But model architecture must support these kernels; we do kernel substitution or fallbacks when needed.
[08:15] Jamal Reed: grouped-query optimization — can you explain?
[08:19] Alex Ramos: it's basically batching queries with shared keys so we compute K/V once and reuse for a group of queries that map to the same document chunk; this reduces repeated attention work. Works well when you have many short queries against same large context.

[08:45] [09:00] Tom Alvarez: what about hardware? does performance scale linearly across instances? we have a mix of A10G and A100s.
[09:08] Maya Singh: A100 gives you more memory and better throughput for dense attention; A10G is cost-effective for smaller models. For 128k contexts memory is the bottleneck, so prefer higher-memory GPUs or multi-GPU sharding. We also have multi-host KV sharding to spread out memory. We'll include recommended instance types in the benchmark spreadsheet.

[09:45] [10:00] Dr. Lila Chen: network egress: for VPC/private we need to ensure no PHI leaves our environment. How do Redwood Private deployments handle encrypt-at-rest and key management?
[10:12] Jordan Park: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and never stores plaintext outside the private cluster. We can deploy control plane in customer VPC and use SAML SSO + audit logs. Sara, Maya will send the compliance pack.
[10:30] Sara Okoye: great, we'll need encryption keys rotation policy and proof of attestation. Also want to see TLS mutual auth for inter-host communications.
[10:40] Alex Ramos: we support mTLS for host-level RPCs, and you can plug in your own HSM for key operations. We'll document the attestation steps.

[11:00] [11:30] Maya Singh: pivoting back to benchmarks: recommended tests — (1) cold-start full 128k ingest then single-query P95 latency, (2) warm run with semantic chunk caching then throughput at target QPS, (3) regression checks across quant levels, (4) tail-latency tests with simulated KV spillover. We'll provide scripts and a runner.
[11:55] Tom Alvarez: can your runner simulate our network config (VPC private subnets, firewall rules)?
[12:01] Maya Singh: yes the runner supports deployment profiles; for on-prem we'll run with your network constraints or provide a dockerized runner you can run in your environment.

[12:20] [12:45] Jordan Park: on monitoring — what metrics are critical?
[12:48] Alex Ramos: token latency breakdown (tokenize -> batch queue -> compute -> kv lookup -> postprocess), cache hit/miss by chunk ID, GPU memory pressure, NVMe spill rates, batch sizes distribution, and per-route cost estimates. We tie these into Redwood Console for dashboards and alerting.

[13:20] [13:40] Dr. Lila Chen: curious about deterministic outputs across quant levels and sharded runs — for audits we need repeatable outputs.
[13:48] Maya Singh: determinism is tricky across quant and multi-host sharded runs. For strict compliance you can pin to a specific model build and disable non-deterministic kernels, and record seeds. We'll also provide evaluation artifacts for audit. There may still be micro differences but we can bound them and tie to regression tests.

[14:10] [14:30] Jamal Reed: any best practices for chunk indexing vs embeddings? We have a vector DB already (we use Pinecone).
[14:36] Maya Singh: if you already have a vector DB use semantic chunking + higher recall retrieval then fetch what you need into the model's KV. The pattern: retrieve top-k chunks by embedding, then order by recency/importance, then attend to top N. That keeps KV small and focused. You can also store compressed summaries in the vector DB to reduce token count.

[15:00] [15:30] Tom Alvarez: what are typical token counts in your field tests for clinical notes? is 128k overkill?
[15:36] Dr. Lila Chen: our combined notes per patient can be 50k–200k tokens depending on imaging reports and raw transcripts. So 128k is a reasonable midline.

[16:00] [16:20] Maya Singh: ok quick demo of a micro-benchmark we ran. (screen share notes) We ran a 128k synthetic patient record, chunked into 16 x 8k chunks, used Q4_0 quant, A100 multi-GPU with KV sharding. Results: cold P95 ~ 4.6s, warm P95 with cache hits ~ 1.2s, throughput sustained ~ 45 qps on batched queries. With Q5_0 throughput bumped another 20% but saw 4% drop on clinical F1.
[16:55] Dr. Lila Chen: numbers look realistic. For our SLA we'd need sub-2s for warm queries; looks feasible with cache sizing.
[17:10] Alex Ramos: note the tail spikes came from NVMe spillbacks when hot-set exceeded GPU memory. We had prefetcher tuned to 2x expected window which reduced spikes.

[17:40] [18:00] Jordan Park: on the pilot — what would success look like?
[18:05] Dr. Lila Chen: three things: (1) warm-query P95 <2s for single-record QA against 128k contexts, (2) <3% degradation vs fp16 on our clinical evals for any quantization used, (3) no PHI exfil — private deployment with customer KMS.
[18:26] Jordan Park: good. we'll commit to those gates for pilot acceptance.

[18:45] [19:05] Tom Alvarez: about cost — what's the unit economics for long-context workloads? rough order of magnitude.
[19:12] Maya Singh: long-context adds proportional GPU time; quant and batching reduce per-token compute. For the workload we discussed, cost per query varies a lot by instance type but expect 3-6x per-token cost vs 4k baseline. We'll give detailed cost modeling in the spreadsheet.

[19:40] [20:00] Sara Okoye: one more security question: do you persist any logs with PHI? we need audit log retention and redaction options.
[20:09] Alex Ramos: by default Private keeps logs in your VPC and you control retention. We offer automated redaction and tokenization hooks; we can also disable transcript retention entirely. We'll share the config options.

[20:40] [21:00] Jordan Park: okay wrapping up: next steps quick recap. Maya to share benchmarks&runner; Alex to send monitoring dashboards and sample alerts; Jordan pricing + SOW; Sara to get compliance pack. Pilot week tentatively week of 2026-09-28.
[21:25] Dr. Lila Chen: sounds good. I'll coordinate internal stakeholders.

[21:40] [22:00] END OF TRANSCRIPT (session continues with minor off-topic items)
